clue.text: Reade's Rhino ?

parts.note: Charles Reade wrote a Victorian novel about money, and rhino is old British slang for money, so the clue asks for the title of Reade's book about it

explanation.surface: A query about a rhinoceros belonging to someone called Reade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhino' is old British slang for money; Charles Reade's 1863 novel 'Hard Cash' is the book meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhino is slang for ready money, which is coins and notes rather than credit, and Reade used that phrase as a novel title.

clue.text: In term time he or she might take it in with mirthful result

definitions.text: In term time he or she might take it in with mirthful result

parts.words: In term time he or she might take it in with mirthful result
parts.note: a university term and a name for either sex are this word, and adding IT inside gives a word for mirth

explanation.surface: A student in term finding something amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hilary term is a term at Oxford; the name suits a man or woman, and taking IT in gives HILARITY.
explanation.definitionFit: A unisex first name and the Oxford spring term share this word.

clue.text: There's always among sappers a disposition to admire

indicators.note: among means the word for always is placed inside the word for sappers

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army corps whose soldiers are called sappers
ever means always

explanation.surface: Army engineers are said to be always ready to look up to others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts EVER inside RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To honour deeply is a stronger synonym of esteem or admire.

clue.text: Study the eloquent in the stream

parts.note: to con is an old verb meaning to study or learn
someone eloquent is fluent in speech

explanation.surface: Learning from the speechmaker while standing in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Streams that flow together merge into one current, so this adjective describes merging flows.

clue.text: Travellers raise their hands in support

definitions.text: Travellers raise their hands in support

parts.words: Travellers raise their hands in support
parts.note: commuters standing on a crowded bus or train reach up to hold the overhead loops for balance

explanation.surface: Voters raising hands to show they back a motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raise their hands in support' suggests a vote, but it means standing passengers gripping overhead straps.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing passengers who hold an overhead loop for balance are called this.

clue.text: Pictures the getaways of yore

explanation.surface: A caption for old photographs of escapes from long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Pictures of views (land- or sea-) are called this, and in old English the word was a shortened form of escapes.

clue.text: Company at one for a furry quadruped

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A firm working as a unit for a furry animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring-tailed raccoon relative of the Americas is a four-footed mammal with fur.

clue.text: The foam Of seas, in faery lands forlorn " (Keats)

definitions.text: The foam Of seas, in faery lands forlorn " (Keats)

parts.words: The foam Of seas, in faery lands forlorn " (Keats)
parts.note: a gap in a line of the Ode to a Nightingale, describing the magic casements opening on dangerous seas

explanation.surface: A line from Keats's nightingale ode with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats wrote 'magic casements, opening on the foam / Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn'; the missing word fills the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's adjective for the seas means full of danger.

clue.text: Nevertheless it looks right in the mirror!

definitions.text: Nevertheless it looks right in the mirror!

parts.words: Nevertheless it looks right in the mirror
parts.note: the Latin word for left-handed appears as right-hand in a mirror image

explanation.surface: Someone checking an outfit in a mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: In heraldry and Latin the word means left; a mirror swaps left and right, so it looks right.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry the term means on the left side, from Latin for left.

clue.text: Scholar, Gypsy, Priest

parts.note: George Borrow's novel of 1851 carries the subtitle The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest, so the three nouns point to its title

explanation.surface: A list of three characters, recalling Arnold's poem The Scholar-Gipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two words suggest Matthew Arnold's 'Scholar-Gipsy', but the whole list is the subtitle of George Borrow's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrow's semi-autobiographical novel bears this title, a Romani word meaning word-master, with that three-part subtitle.

clue.text: Quarters for poor performers ?

parts.note: in British sporting slang a rabbit is a poor player, so the lodging meant is where rabbits live

explanation.surface: A theatrical landlady advertising cheap rooms for struggling actors.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'rabbit' is British slang for a weak player, at cricket especially, so the poor performers are rabbits and their quarters a burrow system.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabbits live in a network of burrows, and rabbit is slang for an inept sportsman.

clue.text: Where barnacles lose their grip

parts.note: ships are taken into dry docks so their hulls can be scraped of barnacles and weed

explanation.surface: Barnacles losing hold of a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: To grave a ship is to clean its bottom, done in a dry dock.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry docks where ships' hulls were cleaned, graved, of barnacles and weed carry this name.

clue.text: Truly a pre-breathalyser test !

parts.note: before breath tests, police asked a suspected drunk to say a tongue-twister, and the word wanted follows truly in it

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned way of checking whether a driver had been drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: Before the breathalyser, a suspected drunk might be asked to say 'truly rural', a tongue-twister hard to manage when tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'truly rural' was the classic sobriety tongue-twister, so the missing word completes it.

clue.text: Celt pairs are uncommonly hard little pieces

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests the letters of the two words are arranged in an unusual way

explanation.surface: Pairs of Celts are rarely tough, it claims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' rearranges CELTPAIRS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny solid fragments, such as specks of grit, are minute bits of matter.

clue.text: Through enterprise, by chance

parts.note: per is Latin for through or by means of
an adventure is a bold undertaking or venture

explanation.surface: Succeeding through enterprise, or merely through luck.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning perhaps or possibly, as in Elizabethan speech.

clue.text: He's more eccentric than alien

indicators.note: eccentric hints that the letters of the two words are arranged oddly

explanation.surface: A man said to be odder than any alien.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges THANALIEN; 'He' defines a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A male first name, so a fitting stand-in for the pronoun meaning a man.

clue.text: " The firmament on high" (Addison)

parts.note: the opening line of Joseph Addison's hymn, with a gap before firmament

explanation.surface: The opening of an Addison hymn with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Addison's hymn begins 'The spacious firmament on high'.
explanation.definitionFit: Addison's adjective for the sky means vast and roomy.

clue.text: The woodwork of Charles's equipage, before tax

indicators.note: before places the wagon word ahead of the tax word

parts.note: Charles's Wain is the old British name for the Plough constellation, and a wain is a wagon or carriage
scot is an old word for a tax, as in scot-free

explanation.surface: Charles's carriage woodwork priced before tax is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooden panelling lining the lower part of a room's walls.

clue.text: They took cognizance of broom

parts.note: a cognizance is a heraldic badge, and a medieval royal house took its name and badge from the broom plant, planta genista

explanation.surface: Some people paying attention to a sweeping brush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cognizance' is a heraldic badge and 'broom' the shrub, Latin planta genista, worn by the English royal house that ruled from Henry II to Richard II.
explanation.definitionFit: The dynasty descended from Geoffrey of Anjou wore a sprig of broom, planta genista, as its badge.

clue.text: Listen, it's so quiet now

indicators.note: now hints that the letters of the word listen have been changed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Telling someone to listen because it has gone quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'now' rearranges LISTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Making no sound is a stronger form of being hushed.

clue.text: Oddly, having got the worst of it

definitions.text: Oddly, having got the worst of it

parts.words: Oddly, having got the worst of it
parts.note: the word sounds like coming out best, yet it describes a loser, which is the oddity

explanation.surface: Someone losing an argument in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: To be bested is to be defeated, which is odd since it contains best.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten or outdone; the loser in a contest has been worsted.

clue.text: Had a powwow and made a donation

explanation.surface: A tribal council met and then gave a gift.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both held a discussion and bestowed something, such as an honour.

clue.text: He's not at home

parts.note: a servant's phrase about a caller suggests someone out, but it means a person banished from his homeland

explanation.surface: A butler turning away a caller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not at home' suggests a butler's excuse, but means living banished from one's country.
explanation.definitionFit: A person banished from their native land lives abroad.

clue.text: Little Girl Blue

parts.note: the little girl of Wonderland shares her name with a pale greenish-blue shade, named after a president's daughter

explanation.surface: The title of a well-known sad song.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the song title; the reading wanted is Carroll's little girl, whose name also prefixes a pale blue shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's heroine is the best-known little girl in fiction, and the same name labels a light blue colour.

clue.text: A flower for the whale that belongs to him

parts.note: orc is an old name for a killer whale or grampus
his is the possessive meaning belonging to him

explanation.surface: Naming a flower after the whale that owns it.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for an orchid, especially a wild one.

clue.text: Where Leyton may look for a rival team?

definitions.text: Where Leyton may look for a rival team?

parts.words: Where Leyton may look for a rival team
parts.note: Leyton's football club is called Orient, so its rival would be the opposite compass region, the West

explanation.surface: A London football club scouting for opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: Leyton Orient is a London football club; the opposite of the Orient (the East) is the West.
explanation.definitionFit: The western world is the opposite of the Orient, the East, so it suits a rival to Orient.

clue.text: It's dogged as does it for you, dear solver !

definitions.text: It's dogged as does it for you, dear solver !

parts.words: It's dogged as does it for you, dear solver
parts.note: the proverb about doggedness is bent to mean a dog breed, and also the person who composes the puzzle for the solver

explanation.surface: Encouragement to a solver to keep going with persistence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's dogged as does it' is a proverb praising persistence; here 'dogged' points to a gundog breed, and the compiler is also given this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A gundog breed and the compiler of a crossword share this name.

clue.text: In a sometimes splendid state of detachment

definitions.text: In a sometimes splendid state of detachment

parts.words: In a sometimes splendid state of detachment
parts.note: Britain's nineteenth-century foreign policy of staying aloof was called splendid isolation, so the word means cut off

explanation.surface: Describing someone grandly aloof from others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splendid isolation' described Britain's late-Victorian policy of avoiding alliances.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cut off and alone is the state the phrase splendid isolation describes.
